identity.title: A Recursive Decomposition Framework for Causal Structure Learning in the Presence of Latent Variables

problem.claim: Constraint-based causal discovery becomes computationally expensive in high-dimensional settings because it relies heavily on conditional-independence testing.

gap.claim: Most existing divide-and-conquer frameworks assume causal sufficiency and therefore do not address latent-variable settings.

contributions.claim: Generalizes divide-and-conquer causal discovery theoretically to settings with latent variables.
Introduces DiCoLa, a recursive decomposition framework that divides global learning into smaller subproblems and combines their solutions through principled reconstruction.
Reports soundness and completeness results for the proposed framework.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish DiCoLa as a divide-and-conquer framework designed to operate with latent variables, beyond the usual causal-sufficiency assumption.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that synthetic-data experiments show significant computational-efficiency improvements across a range of causal discovery algorithms.
The authors report that experiments on a real-world dataset illustrate the method’s practical effectiveness.
The authors report theoretically established soundness and completeness of the framework.

narrative_sequence.summary: High-dimensional constraint-based discovery is computationally costly because of extensive conditional-independence testing.
Existing divide-and-conquer approaches generally rely on causal sufficiency, leaving latent-variable settings insufficiently addressed.
The paper proposes DiCoLa, which recursively solves smaller subproblems and reconstructs the global causal structure.
The authors report soundness and completeness, synthetic efficiency gains, and a real-world demonstration.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a computational bottleneck with a limiting structural assumption, then introduces a recursive decomposition and reconstruction mechanism to address both.

lessons.interpretation: This pairing makes the method’s purpose and claimed scope easy to trace from problem to design.
lessons.application: When presenting a new algorithm, explicitly connect each major design component to a named bottleneck or assumption, then state how local outputs are recombined globally.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the method has no meaningful decomposition or when local solutions cannot be principledly integrated.

unknowns: No efficiency metrics, baselines, dataset details, algorithm list, or experimental conditions are provided.
The abstract does not specify the formal assumptions or meanings of soundness and completeness.
